passage: When the Pune school merged Class 9A and 9C for the science fair, Irawati Ma'am hoped the old rivalry would fade. It didn't. The head of department had named only 9A students as team leaders, with 9C as "helpers." Within a week the 9A kids joked that 9C couldn't wire a bulb, and 9C sat in a silent block at the back. Asif, from 9C, stopped coming to the lab at all. Irawati watched and saw what was wrong: same room, no common aim, one side in charge. She went to the principal. Together they reshuffled everything: mixed teams of four, two from each section, rotating leaders, one prize per team. The principal announced it at assembly. By the fair, Asif was explaining his team's solar oven to the judges, with a 9A boy holding the chart and nodding.

qa.q: What did the head of department name only 9A students as?
qa.a: Team leaders.

qa.q: How did Irawati Ma'am feel after watching the first week, and what did she realise?
qa.a: She was likely disappointed that the rivalry hadn't faded, and realised that the same room with no common aim and one side in charge was making it worse.

qa.q: What choices did Irawati Ma'am and the principal make, and why did they help?
qa.a: They made mixed teams of four with rotating leaders and one prize per team, announced at assembly, so students worked as equals toward a shared goal with backing from the top.

qa.q: What was the first week like for Asif, and what had changed for him by the fair?
qa.a: As a 'helper' mocked by 9A, Asif felt pushed out and stopped coming; by the fair he was explaining his team's solar oven with a 9A partner beside him.

grounding: A teacher sees that mixing rival sections with unequal roles and no shared aim hardens stereotypes, then gets equal teams, a common goal and the principal's backing.

passage: "You look like you've swallowed a lemon, Himani." Pallavi pushed a cup of tea across the staffroom table. "The friendship day with the other school. Disaster." "What happened?" "We put our girls and their girls in one hall for an hour. No task, just 'mingle.' Ours sat on one side, theirs on the other. Then one of ours said their school didn't even have a proper lab, and it got nasty." "So mixing made it worse." "Mixing like that did. Nobody had a reason to need anyone. And our girls were introduced as the 'hosts', as if they were doing them a favour." "What would you do instead?" Himani set down her cup. "Mixed teams, a real job, a heritage walk they plan together, equal roles. And both principals standing there saying it matters." "Write it up. I'll sign it."

qa.q: How long were the two schools' girls put in one hall?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: Why does Himani think the friendship day failed?
qa.a: Himani thinks nobody had a reason to need anyone, and calling one side 'hosts' made it unequal, so the contact only hardened the split.

qa.q: What does Himani plan instead, and why should it work better?
qa.a: Mixed teams planning a heritage walk together with equal roles and both principals backing it, so students work as equals toward a shared aim.

qa.q: How might the visiting school's girls have felt being treated as guests receiving a favour?
qa.a: They may have felt looked down on and defensive, which made the remark about the lab cut deeper and kept them on their side of the hall.

grounding: A teacher sees that bringing two schools' students together with no shared task and unequal status hardens stereotypes, and plans equal teams with a common aim and authority backing.

passage: I'm Irfan, and I've coached the school football team for three years. My worst idea came last spring. The boarders and the day scholars had been sniping at each other for months, so I made them share one practice. But I let the boarders play the match while the day scholars ran drills on the side. Within a week, Pooja, one of my best day-scholar players, was calling the boarders "the rich kids," and they were calling her lot "the bus crowd." I'd put them on the same field and made it worse. So I changed three things. Every team got an equal mix. Every drill needed both groups to score. And the principal came to watch, which told everyone this mattered. By June, Pooja was passing to a boarder for the winning goal, and nobody was keeping count of who was who.

qa.q: What did the day scholars do while the boarders played the match?
qa.a: They ran drills on the side.

qa.q: What did Irfan realise after a week of shared practice?
qa.a: Irfan realised that putting the groups on the same field with unequal roles had made the rivalry worse, not better.

qa.q: Which three changes did Irfan make, and why did they work?
qa.a: Equal mixes on every team, drills needing both groups to score, and the principal watching; together they gave equal status, a shared goal and visible backing.

qa.q: How might Pooja's view of the boarders have changed by June?
qa.a: From 'the rich kids' to teammates she could trust with a winning pass, because they now needed each other to score.

grounding: A coach sees that sharing a field with unequal roles hardens a rivalry, then uses equal teams, shared goals and the principal's support to reduce it.

passage:
Teacher's note, library period, 18 July. Written by Elizabeth, librarian.
The management combined the English-medium and Kannada-medium Class 9 sections for the library period this term, hoping they would mix. They haven't. There is no shared task; they are only told to read quietly. And the English-medium students were made library monitors, so they check the others' books in and out.
Within a month the monitors call the others slow, and the Kannada-medium group sits by the far window muttering about snobs. Rafiq, a monitor, told me the other side "doesn't even try". Nothing in that room gives him a reason to think otherwise.
Sitting in one room is not the same as meeting.
Next: I've asked the principal to back a joint school newspaper, with mixed teams, equal editor roles for both sections and one deadline everyone must meet. The principal has agreed to announce it at assembly.

qa.q: What role were the English-medium students given in the library?
qa.a: They were made library monitors.

qa.q: How does Rafiq seem to feel about the other group, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq seems to feel superior as a monitor, and with no equal, shared work in the library, that distance has hardened his stereotype.

qa.q: What went wrong with the combined period, and what does Elizabeth propose?
qa.a: There was no shared task and the roles were unequal; Elizabeth proposes a joint newspaper with mixed teams, equal editors, one deadline and the principal's backing.

qa.q: How might the Kannada-medium students experience being checked in and out by monitors?
qa.a: They may feel looked down on and controlled, which pushes them to the far window and to calling the others snobs.

grounding: A librarian notices that putting two sections in one room with no shared goal and unequal roles hardens stereotypes, and plans equal, goal-driven contact backed by the principal.

passage:
Monday, 10 pm
The unity assembly was a mistake, and I planned it. Class 10A and 10B have fought over the cricket ground all year, so I put both sections in the hall for a talk on friendship. 10A, the head boy's section, were made ushers and seated 10B at the back. No task, no reason to speak to each other, only a speech.
By lunch the 10B boys were using "the ushers" as an insult, and someone had scrawled something rude on 10A's board. Worse than before.
Salma, who teaches geography, said over tea, "They were in the same room, but not on the same side. Give them one job they can only finish together, and make them equals."
So: a joint wall map of the town for Founders' Day. Mixed pairs, both sections leading equally. The headmaster has agreed to open it himself.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did the 10B boys start using as an insult?
qa.a: They started using 'the ushers' as an insult.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel about the unity assembly now?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels regretful and responsible, since Chaitanya planned the assembly and it left the two sections worse than before.

qa.q: What is Chaitanya's new plan, and why might it work better?
qa.a: A joint wall map with mixed pairs, equal leadership and the headmaster's support, so the two sections need each other and work as equals.

qa.q: Why might Salma's view of the assembly differ from what Chaitanya first expected?
qa.a: Salma saw that sitting together without a shared goal or equal status doesn't build friendship, while Chaitanya had hoped the talk alone would.

grounding: A teacher sees that seating rival sections together with unequal roles and no shared goal only hardened hostility, and plans equal, cooperative contact backed by the headmaster.

passage: In the small-town school near Kottayam, the boys from the upper village and the lower village had been fighting all term over the football ground. Joseph, the PE teacher, tried a fix: put both groups in the same detention room after school. The upper-village boys were made monitors because their marks were better. Joseph watched through the window. Nobody talked. The monitors wrote the lower-village boys' names on the board for "noise." One lower-village boy muttered, "See? They always think they're bosses." By Friday the fights were worse. Joseph sat with the headmistress, Gurleen ma'am. "I made it worse," he said. "Same room, no reason to cooperate, and I handed one side power." She nodded. "Then give them a reason." They planned a single inter-school football team: mixed, captain chosen by vote, the district cup as the goal.

qa.q: Why were the upper-village boys made monitors?
qa.a: They were made monitors because their marks were better.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he said "I made it worse"?
qa.a: Joseph felt regretful and troubled, realising his plan had hardened the rivalry instead of easing it.

qa.q: Why is a single mixed football team with a voted captain a better plan?
qa.a: It gives both groups a common goal, equal status and the school's support, which are the conditions under which contact reduces prejudice.

qa.q: How might the lower-village boys have seen the detention room?
qa.a: They likely felt humiliated and controlled, which confirmed their belief that the upper-village boys always act like bosses.

grounding: A teacher sees that bringing rival groups together with unequal status and no shared aim only hardens stereotypes, and plans equal, goal-based teamwork instead.

passage: After a fight between students who supported rival Lisbon football clubs, the school tried a "unity lunch." Ines, the form teacher, watched it from the canteen doorway. The two groups were placed at the same long table with no plan, no task, and the kids from the club with the bigger stadium were handed the serving spoons. Within ten minutes, jokes turned into chants. Jana, a quiet fifteen-year-old from the smaller club's side, put down her fork and left. Ines followed her into the corridor. "They made us wait for them to serve us," Jana said, blinking fast. "Like we're guests in their house." Ines didn't argue. She went back and thought about what had happened. Sitting together had only proved each side's stories. What they needed was a problem neither could solve alone, like the school film project, with equal roles and the head's support.

qa.q: What did the kids from the club with the bigger stadium get handed?
qa.a: They were handed the serving spoons.

qa.q: What was Ines thinking as she went back to the canteen?
qa.a: Ines felt troubled and reflective, realising the lunch had only confirmed each side's stories because it lacked a shared aim and equality.

qa.q: What could make the next mixing attempt work?
qa.a: A shared project like the school film, with equal roles and the head's backing, would give the groups a real reason to depend on each other.

qa.q: How did Jana experience the unity lunch?
qa.a: Jana felt humiliated and unwelcome, like a guest waiting to be served in someone else's house.

grounding: A teacher notices that bringing rival groups together without a shared goal and with unequal roles hardens stereotypes, and considers equal, goal-based contact.

passage:
At the Delhi school, Ishita Ma'am had tried a "harmony week". She'd put Class 10A, mostly from the rich colony, and 10C, mostly scholarship students from the nearby basti, in the same hall to "mix". No task, no teams.
Within an hour, 10A sat on the chairs and 10C on the floor. Some 10A boys mocked 10C's shoes. Vasudha, a 10C girl, walked out crying.
Ishita Ma'am felt sick. The mixing had made things worse.
The next week she tried again, differently. Mixed teams of four, each with equal roles, building a model for the science fair. The principal came to announce a prize. Teams had to depend on each other.
By Friday, Vasudha and a 10A girl were laughing over their model.

qa.q: What did some 10A boys mock?
qa.a: They mocked 10C's shoes.

qa.q: How did Ishita Ma'am feel after the first harmony week?
qa.a: She felt sick and upset, seeing that the mixing without a shared task had made things worse.

qa.q: What changed in the second attempt, and why did it work?
qa.a: Mixed teams with equal roles, a common goal for the science fair and backing from the principal, so students depended on each other as equals.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt after the first week?
qa.a: Vasudha probably felt humiliated and hurt, walking out crying.

grounding: A teacher sees that mixing groups without a shared goal or equal status hardens stereotypes, and that equal teams with a common aim help.

passage:
Dear Pema,
You asked about my "mixing" experiment with the two rival sections in Class 9. Honestly, the first try was a disaster.
I put 9A and 9B together in one room for a free period, hoping they'd get along. No task. No roles. 9A sat on one side, 9B on the other. By the end, there were insults about "backbenchers" and "toppers", and one fight.
I felt terrible. I'd made it worse.
Then I read about working together as equals. Next time, I made mixed pairs for the inter-house quiz, with the principal backing it and a real prize. Each pair needed both people's knowledge.
Last week, a 9A girl and a 9B boy won together and hugged.
Ayesha

qa.q: What were the insults about in the first try?
qa.a: About "backbenchers" and "toppers".

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel after the first experiment?
qa.a: Ayesha felt terrible, having made the rivalry worse.

qa.q: What made the second attempt work?
qa.a: Mixed pairs with equal roles, a shared goal in the quiz, a real prize and the principal's backing.

qa.q: How might the students in the winning pair feel about each other now?
qa.a: They probably feel closer and proud, having won together and hugged.

grounding: A teacher sees that mixing rival sections without a shared goal hardens stereotypes, and that equal pairs with a common aim help.

passage:
"You asked why I stopped 'friendship days' at my school. I'm Minakshi, and I teach Class 8 in Guwahati.
We had two groups who didn't get along: kids from the hill villages and kids from the town. The old principal thought just putting them together in assembly would fix it. It didn't. The town kids sat in front. The hill kids stood at the back. Jokes got worse.
So I tried something else. I made mixed teams for the school's clean-water project, equal roles, one goal: a working rainwater system. The new principal backed it and gave them the school's roof.
One boy, Ojas, a town kid, used to mock the hill kids' accent. By the end, he was listening to a hill girl explain the pipes.
Being in a room isn't enough. They have to need each other."

qa.q: What did the mixed teams build?
qa.a: A working rainwater system.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel about the old principal's approach?
qa.a: Minakshi felt it was not enough and saw that it made the jokes worse.

qa.q: Why did the clean-water project work better than assemblies?
qa.a: It gave mixed teams equal roles, one shared goal and the principal's backing, so they needed each other.

qa.q: How did Ojas's attitude change?
qa.a: Ojas went from mocking the hill kids' accent to listening to a hill girl explain the pipes.

grounding: A teacher sees that mixing groups without a shared aim hardens stereotypes, and that equal teams with a common goal soften them.

passage: I'm Devika, and I teach Class 9 at a school that merged two sections this year: the fee-paying students and the students on free government seats. The principal, Ramesh Sir, sat them in the same room and called it integration. I watched it fail for a month. The fee-paying children got the front benches and the monitor posts; the free-seat children sat at the back. There was no project they had to do together, nothing either side needed from the other. The mockery grew: 'backbenchers', 'scholarship types'. In the staff room I heard a colleague say, 'See, they don't mix.' I don't think the children were the problem. I think the room was. So I asked Ramesh Sir for three changes: mixed project teams, rotating monitors and a clear rule against mocking. He agreed to a term's trial.

qa.q: What did the fee-paying students get?
qa.a: The front benches and the monitor posts.

qa.q: What did Devika feel watching the merged class for a month?
qa.a: Devika felt troubled and frustrated, seeing mockery grow while others blamed the children.

qa.q: Why are Devika's three changes likely to work better?
qa.a: Mixed teams give a shared goal, rotating monitors give equal status, and a rule against mocking shows backing from authority.

qa.q: What is it like for the free-seat students at the back of the room?
qa.a: They are likely to feel excluded and looked down on, mocked as backbenchers with no equal role.

grounding: A teacher sees that merely seating two groups together, unequal and with no shared goal, hardens stereotypes.

passage:
Week one: Hemant, the sports teacher, arranged a friendly football match between his school and the rival school across the river, hoping the boys would get along. It was a disaster. Each side sat apart, the referee was from Hemant's school, and when Varun scored for the rivals, someone shouted, 'Cheaters, like always.' Two boys shoved each other.
Week two: in the staff room Hemant sat with his notebook. Same pitch, same afternoon, but no shared goal, and one side held all the power, even the whistle. No wonder it hardened things.
Week five: he tried again with the other school's coach. This time they formed mixed teams for a district tournament, players from both schools on each side, co-captains, a neutral referee, and both principals came to watch. By the semi-final, Varun was passing to boys who had shoved him a month earlier.

qa.q: Who was the referee in week one?
qa.a: The referee was from Hemant's school.

qa.q: What did Hemant feel in the staff room during week two?
qa.a: Hemant felt disappointed and reflective, realising his well-meant match had only hardened the rivalry.

qa.q: What changes made the second attempt work?
qa.a: Mixed teams with a common goal, co-captains for equal status, a neutral referee and both principals showing support.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt when someone shouted 'Cheaters, like always'?
qa.a: Varun probably felt insulted and angry, his goal turned into proof of an old stereotype.

grounding: Over five weeks a sports teacher sees rival-school contact fail without equal status or a shared goal, then succeed with both.

passage: Harsha, you want to put the Hindi-medium and English-medium sections together for annual day and 'let them mix'. Let me tell you what happened when I tried that in 1989, at a girls' school in Mangalore. I put both sections in one hall to rehearse: English-medium girls on stage with the lines, Kannada-medium girls in the chorus at the back. No shared goal, just one group decorating the other's show. By the third day they had names for each other. One girl cried in the washroom. I thought mixing would do the magic. It made things worse. The next year, Elizabeth Teacher got wiser. I gave them one play to write together, in both languages, with equal parts and one rule: no mocking, or you're out. The principal sat in on rehearsals. That play is still the best thing I ever directed.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth try this in 1989?
qa.a: At a girls' school in Mangalore.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when a girl cried in the washroom?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt dismayed and guilty, realising the hoped-for mixing had made things worse.

qa.q: The next year Elizabeth gave both sections one play to write together, with equal parts. Why was that a turning point?
qa.a: It gave the girls a shared goal and equal status, with clear backing from the principal, so contact built respect instead of names.

qa.q: What was it like for the Kannada-medium girls in the back chorus?
qa.a: They probably felt looked down on and unequal, decorating someone else's show, which bred resentment.

grounding: A senior teacher recalls contact between two groups failing without shared goals or equal roles, and what worked instead.

passage: With annual exams three weeks away and the staff room short of teachers, the principal merged 9A and 9D for revision classes. Baljeet Sir, taking the combined group, did as he was told: 9A, "the toppers", sat in front as group leaders; 9D sat at the back to be helped. By day three the room was split like a border. Kamal, from 9D, stopped bringing his notebook. "They talk to us like servants," he muttered. Someone from 9A called out "back benchers" loudly, and nobody stopped it. Baljeet Sir watched the gap widen. That night he rewrote the plan: mixed pairs, each pair owning one chapter to teach the whole class, and a rule, cleared with the principal, that mockery meant losing your chapter. On Monday Kamal and Riddhi from 9A stood up together to explain photosynthesis.

qa.q: Which two sections were merged for revision classes?
qa.a: 9A and 9D.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Sir realise as he watched the room split?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and responsible, seeing that seating 9A as leaders over 9D with no shared aim was hardening the labels instead of easing them.

qa.q: Why is Baljeet Sir's new plan more likely to work?
qa.a: Mixed pairs work as equals toward a shared goal, teaching a chapter, with the principal backing a rule against mockery.

qa.q: What was it like for Kamal to sit at the back as someone to be helped?
qa.a: Kamal felt looked down on, like a servant, and pulled away by no longer bringing his notebook.

grounding: A teacher sees that mixing two sections with unequal status and no shared goal hardens stereotypes, and switches to equal pairs with a common aim and backing.
